newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Last governor sees HK democracy as irreversible.
newsitem.headline: Last governor sees HK democracy as irreversible.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten fired a parting shot at Hong Kong's future ruler China on Thursday by declaring democratic changes irreversible.

But leader-in-waiting Tung Chee-hwa unveiled a bill to erase doubts about the legality of his measures diluting democracy and civil liberties after Britain hands its 156-year-old colony back to communist-ruled Beijing at midnight on June 30, 12 days away.
Meanwhile, a new survey showed more of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people are happy about their imminent return to China and most prefer to stay in the bustling capitalist territory.
"It seems to me unlikely that a change of approach or attitude is going to suddenly reverse what has been happening," Patten told the colony's flagship English-language newspaper.

The 28th and last British governor told the South China Morning Post he expected "a great deal more emphasis on continuity" by Tung, who was chosen by a China-assembled committee last December, after the change of flag.
Tung's office meanwhile circulated an "umbrella" bill to be passed shortly after midnight by the provisional legislature in order to protect his controversial legislation.
The "reunification bill" will confirm the legality of a string of laws the body has adopted in advance of the handover, in order to avert any later court challenge to their legitimacy.

These include curbs on protest rights and foreign funding of political groups. New election rules are also being served up, reversing Patten reforms of the past five years which broadened the democratic franchise.
"It is necessary for completing the legislative procedure that the laws passed by the provisional legislature before July 1 should be ratified," Tung's spokesman said.

"There is no doubt about the validity of the laws but the confirmation process would serve as an added assurance. It would be beneficial to the public to be given account of all the laws passed by the provisional legislature before July 1."
Hong Kong's highly popular Democratic Party plans to challenge the laws, arguing that the provisional body usurped the powers of the present elected Legislative Council.
The party is excluded from the interim body and faces a political wilderness on July 1, when its legislators will become jobless until they can compete in elections under new rules next year.

Patten said his successors could help mould public opinion but it would take a "brave man, or a very great man or woman, who thinks you can completely reverse social, economic, political processes which have been deep-rooted".
He denied he brought an entirely new political culture to Hong Kong that allowed a more open government and civil service and included democratic reforms that upset China.
"I don't think I brought that into Hong Kong. I think I responded to what was already happening in Hong Kong," he said.
"There's an absurd argument that people in Hong Kong aren't interested in civil liberties, that somehow I introduced alien Western concepts to Hong Kong.

"The tens of thousands of people at Victoria Park the other night are the most eloquent response to that," he said, referring to huge crowds at Hong Kong's June 4 commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen massacre in Beijing.

It has been a sour run-up to Chinese rule, with constant spats between China and Britain and the Hong Kong democrats over the future of democracy and human rights, and the role of the incoming People's Liberation Army garrison.
China sought to play down a row this week over charges that its troops have won special customs privileges.
Another row is simmering behind the scenes over Chinese demands to send PLA units into Hong Kong before July 1.

Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement kept up the pressure on Chinese authorities, staging an anti-PLA protest on Wednesday and vowing to mar the glitzy handover ceremonies with protests and an invasion of the legislature.
